title: OS essentials for backend engineers
subtitle: Processes, threads, memory, files and system calls are where your code meets the machine. Know them, and many "random" production failures stop being random.

c.v: This is a made-up example, but each part of it is common. A team moves a Java order service into Kubernetes. The container gets a 512 MiB memory limit. To be safe, they set the JVM heap to 512 MiB too.
Under load, the pod restarts every few hours.
. The last state has exit code 137. The Kubernetes docs show exactly this pattern: a container goes over its limit, gets killed, restarts, and gets killed again.
The team looks at the JVM dashboard. Heap use is at 400 MiB, well under 512 MiB. So who used the memory?
The answer is: the operating system counted more than the heap. The limit applies to the whole container. It counts every
It even counts file pages in the

A week later, the same service fails in a new way. Logs fill with "too many open files". A client library forgot to close sockets. This lesson explains both failures, and the OS ideas behind them.
Your program cannot use devices such as disks and network cards directly. The
sits in between. It shares the CPU, memory and disks among many programs.

The kernel also keeps limits. It limits how much memory a group of processes may use, and how many files one process may hold open. Some limits are hard. When you hit the memory limit or the open-file limit, the kernel does not slow down politely. It kills the process, or the call fails.

Your runtime shows you a small part of the picture, such as the heap. The kernel counts much more: almost all memory, every open file and socket, and time spent waiting. Limits and costs come from the kernel's view, not your runtime's view.
User mode, kernel mode and system calls
. In user mode it cannot do I/O or other privileged operations. The kernel runs in kernel mode, with full access to the machine.
To ask the kernel for something, a program runs a special trap instruction. The CPU jumps into the kernel, which does the work and then returns to user mode.
The kernel shares each CPU among many threads. It runs one for a while, then switches to another. To switch, it saves the registers of the running thread and restores those of the next one. This is a
Both steps cost time. In 1996, on a 200 MHz CPU, a system call took about 4 microseconds and a context switch about 6.
OSTEP says modern 2–3 GHz systems reach sub-microsecond results.
These are the direct costs. OSTEP also notes that many OS operations depend on memory speed, which has not improved as fast as CPUs.
A few microseconds is cheap once. It is not cheap 100,000 times per second, so reading a file 1 byte per call is slow.

So every address your program prints is a virtual address.
Two processes can use the same address and never see each other's data. This is how the OS keeps one buggy process from damaging another.

c.v: When a pod restarts, check the last state first. The reason
means the container hit its memory limit. The cause can be a limit that is too low, or a memory leak. Trust the reason, not the exit code alone.
Set the memory limit above the heap. Measure total container memory under load, not only heap graphs.
counts warn you before a kill. Any
Treat "too many open files" as a leak until proven otherwise. Raising the limit only buys time.
Count open descriptors per process in your dashboards, next to memory.
Ask "where does this write become durable?" in every design review that stores data.
"Here is our Kubernetes deployment and JVM flags. Estimate total container memory: heap, thread stacks, metaspace and native buffers. Tell me if the memory limit leaves enough room."
"Search this Go service for every place we open a file, socket or HTTP response body. For each, show where it is closed, and list paths where it is not."
"This code writes an order to a file and then replies 'saved'. Explain which crash could lose the order, and show the smallest fix with fsync."
Every memory number the agent gives is labelled heap, stack or native. Totals that add only the heap are wrong.

q.v: Your Java service has a 512 MiB heap. Its container has a 512 MiB memory limit. Why can it still be OOM-killed?

options.v: The limit counts all the memory of the container, such as thread stacks and native buffers, not only the heap.
It cannot. The heap is the only memory a process uses.
Kubernetes kills any container that uses more than half its limit.

why.v: The cgroup counts the memory of every process in it, not only the heap. Each thread has its own stack, and the JVM also uses native memory. The kernel can free page cache, but not these.

q.v: A service logs "too many open files" (EMFILE). What has it hit?

options.v: The per-process limit on open file descriptors, RLIMIT_NOFILE.

why.v: The open(2) man page defines EMFILE as reaching the per-process limit on open file descriptors. A new socket is a file descriptor too.

q.v: write() returned success. Then the machine lost power. Is the data safe?

options.v: Yes. write() returns only after the disk has the data.
Yes, if the file was opened for writing.
Not for sure. write() may only have copied the data to the page cache. Calling fsync() makes it wait for the device.

why.v: The write(2) man page says a successful write gives no guarantee that the data is on disk. fsync() returns only after the device confirms it has stored the data.

q.v: Two threads in the same process open files. What do they share?

options.v: Nothing. Each thread has its own memory and its own file descriptors.
Heap memory and the table of open file descriptors. Each thread has its own stack.

why.v: The pthreads(7) man page lists shared memory, open file descriptors and resource limits, and says each thread has its own stack.
